#6493. A giant planet stopped crossing its star while astronomers watched, and it never left

Astronomers saw a planet around a single star stop crossing it, a first. A hidden neighbor is likely tipping its orbit.

Astronomers had been watching a giant planet pass in front of its star for years. Then, in March 2026, it stopped showing up.

The planet, TOI-2535 b, hasn’t gone anywhere. Its orbit has tipped, most likely from the pull of a second planet in the same system, one that astronomers haven’t detected directly.

TOI-2535 b, more than 1,000 light-years away, is the first confirmed planet around a single star that astronomers have seen stop crossing. Samuel Yee, a 51 Pegasi b Postdoctoral Fellow at UCLA, led the work with UCLA astrophysicist Erik Petigura.

Each of those crossings is called a transit. “The planet’s orbit is tilting so quickly that its transit disappeared while we were watching,” Yee said.

When a planet passes between its star and Earth, it blocks a little of the starlight. The star dims for a few hours, and that small dip is how NASA’s Transiting Exoplanet Survey Satellite (TESS) finds new worlds.

A transit only shows up if the star, the planet and Earth line up almost perfectly. If the orbit tips by just a few degrees, the planet passes above or below the star as seen from Earth, and the star never dims.

TESS checked on the star, called TOI-2535, five times between April 2019 and March 2026.

The planet orbiting it is a hot Jupiter, a gas giant that orbits very close to its star. It goes around once every 8.24 days. Mercury takes 88 days, more than 10 times as long.

To confirm the planet, the team used an instrument on the 11.5-foot (3.5-meter) WIYN telescope at Kitt Peak National Observatory in Arizona. It tracked how the star shifted back and forth, and the measurements ruled out a small star.

Most planets that cross their stars keep a steady schedule. TOI-2535 b’s crossings came as much as six hours early or late. No hot Jupiter that circles its star in under 10 days has a bigger timing swing on record.

Each crossing was also a little shorter than the last, and each one dimmed the star a little less.

A planet blocks less light, for less time, as its path moves from the middle of a star toward its edge.

Over seven years, the path likely moved across more than half of the star’s face. It passed the middle, grazed the edge, then missed the star entirely.

From the ground, the team tried 15 times and caught a crossing only six times, because the planet kept arriving when it wasn’t expected.

When TESS looked again in March 2026, it found no crossing anywhere in the window where the planet could have shown up.

So what’s pulling on it? Planets in the same system tug on each other. If two orbits are tilted relative to one another, those tugs slowly swing the direction each orbit faces.

The team’s computer models suggest the neighbor is at least as massive as Saturn, so it’s probably a second giant planet. The two likely move in a simple rhythm, such as one circling twice for every lap of the other.

By the models, the two orbits must be tilted at least 5 degrees apart to turn this fast.

In most tightly packed systems, orbits stay within 1 to 2 degrees of each other. If this tilt holds up, the system will be one of only a handful so far out of line.

“We think of the universe as resembling clockwork, where everything is regular, but that’s not true. If there are multiple planets in a system, they can affect each other’s orbits,” Yee said.

“We know of a few systems that are like this. This is the most extreme example we’ve seen because the two planets are interacting so strongly.”

Petigura used Earth’s moon to explain it.

“If the moon’s orbit around the Earth was perfectly aligned with the Earth’s orbit around the sun, we would see an eclipse every month,” Petigura said.

“But because the moon’s orbit is tilted, eclipses are less common. The tilt of the moon’s orbit is a relic of its violent formation history, which resulted from a collision with the early Earth.”

The same geometry decides when TOI-2535 b will be back. The team calculated that each orbit goes through a full cycle every 30 to 50 years.

The researchers expect the planet to start crossing its star again within that span. Its hidden neighbor could start crossing even sooner.

Early planet formation models suggested giant planets need lots of ice to form. So hot Jupiters probably formed far from their stars and moved closer later.

How? Yee and Petigura see two ways. One is violent. A near-collision knocks the planet onto a stretched-out orbit, and the star pulls it in.

The other is slow. The planet drifts inward with other planets through the gas and dust around a young star. This way should leave the orbits flat.

TOI-2535 b has a close giant neighbor, so it couldn’t have come the violent way, the team wrote.

“Because TOI-2535 b has a close neighbor, it probably migrated by slowly spiraling in instead of getting flung in,” Yee said. “We may be seeing a formation channel that doesn’t happen very often but is very interesting.”

The tilt is still a loose end. The researchers think parts of the system may have tugged on each other later, tipping the orbits over time.

Hundreds of hot Jupiters are known around other stars. Few have a planet close enough to change their orbits. When one does, the neighbor is almost always much smaller. The only other known exception is WASP-148.

The team can’t say how massive the neighbor is or where it orbits. The crossing times also scattered more than the models predicted.

The star’s back-and-forth motion was jumpier than expected for an old, calm star, too. Both clues could mean there’s more than one unseen planet.

TESS’s first four years of data alone couldn’t have clearly shown the shrinking crossings.

With no crossings left to time, the researchers wrote that the best way forward is to measure the star’s back-and-forth motion often. A neighbor as heavy as the models suggest should show up in that data on its own.

The full study was published in the journal The Astrophysical Journal Letters.

#6492. Most transgender youth satisfied after choosing hormone therapy

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

Taking gender-affirming hormone therapy was the right decision for 97 percent surveyed

Demonstrators rally at the U.S. Supreme Court in 2025 in support of gender-affirming health care for transgender youth. The vast majority of transgender and gender diverse young people are satisfied with their decision to take hormone therapy, according the largest survey on the topic.

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

An overwhelming percentage of transgender and gender diverse young people in the United States express satisfaction with gender-affirming hormone therapy.

Almost 400 transgender and gender diverse young people reflected on their decision to take hormone therapy in the largest such survey to date. Nearly 97 percent affirmed it was the right decision, researchers report November 9 in JAMA Pediatrics. Only about 3 percent, or 10 individuals, said they regretted the step, and of those, seven felt the experience was harmful.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

With concerns around youth well-being fueling limits on gender-affirming hormone therapy, the researchers write, “the results provide further support for the existing standards of care [and] do not support efforts to categorically restrict or ban access.”

Gender-affirming hormone therapy — with the masculinizing hormone testosterone or the feminizing hormone estrogen — allows a person’s body to better match their gender identity. Around 3 percent of 13- to 17-year-olds in the United States identify as transgender.

Among the study’s 376 young people, who were former patients of a clinic for transgender and gender diverse youth, nearly 92 percent began hormones at 17 or younger. Thirty percent took estrogen and 70 percent took testosterone, with the amount of time since starting the hormones averaging five years.

As per clinical guidelines for transgender health care, young people interested in medical treatment, joined by parents or guardians, began with an assessment visit with a mental health professional. For the study, participants took a yearly survey, filled out anytime from one month prior to six months following the anniversary of this initial visit. The research team analyzed surveys submitted from 2023 to 2025.

The new research adds to growing evidence on the benefits of gender-affirming hormone therapy for transgender young people. Gender-affirming hormones improve the alignment these young people experience between their appearance and their gender, increase their satisfaction with life and reduce depression and anxiety.

But state bans have curtailed young people’s access to gender-affirming care, which can include hormone therapy and puberty blockers. As of November 2026 in the United States, 28 states have laws or policies that limit this care, according to the health policy organization KFF. More than half of transgender young people age 13 to 17 reside in states that restrict gender-affirming care. The American Academy of Pediatrics and the Endocrine Society support gender-affirming health care for young people and provide evidence-backed guidelines for treatment.

#6491. Why researchers are paying attention to the jolt you feel just as you drift off

A new survey links frequent sleep starts, the sudden jolts that can happen as you drift off, to poorer sleep, more severe insomnia, and greater anxiety.

Most people have felt it: the sudden jerk as sleep arrives, a leg kick or a whole-body twitch, sometimes with a falling feeling that snaps the eyes open.

In a new survey, people who reported weekly sleep starts along with at least one other symptom reported poorer sleep than those who rarely or never had them.

They also report worse insomnia, more unhelpful beliefs about sleep, and more anxiety.

The survey was online and the answers were self-reported, so it can show a pattern and not a cause. The authors wrote that the jolts and the worry may feed each other, but their data can’t say which comes first.

Tanja Grünberger and Manuel Schabus of the University of Salzburg in Austria led the work with colleagues there.

Sleep researchers call the jolt a hypnic jerk or a sleep start.

Studies that have wired people up while they doze put it in the drowsy stretch between waking and light sleep. The recordings show a brief burst of muscle activity and often a faster heartbeat.

The 96 people in the survey who had sleep starts weekly described far more than a twitch. Muscle jerks were the most common feature, reported by 87.5%.

About two-thirds described a sensation of falling or losing balance, and about the same share reported tingling or numbness.

Nearly half had felt something like an electric shock, 47.9% had seen flashes with their eyes closed, and 21.9% had heard a loud bang that wasn’t there.

Dream-like images, often of falling, went with the jolt for 74%.

The feelings that came with the jolt were mostly unpleasant. Alarm and confusion followed for about four in five participants, and panic for 71.9%. Even so, 95.8% said they usually fell back asleep quickly.

The researchers recruited 194 adults in Austria and Germany, mostly women, with an average age of about 33. Anyone reporting restless legs, sleep apnea, epilepsy or similar conditions was left out.

Ninety-six of them reported jolting awake at least weekly plus at least one other symptom. The other 98 served as the comparison group.

On standard questionnaires, the weekly group scored worse on sleep quality and on insomnia severity.

They held stronger unhelpful beliefs about sleep, rated sleep as more important to them, and scored higher on anxiety and depression.

The weekly group also took longer to fall asleep and slept slightly less.

Daytime sleepiness was the one measure that did not differ between the groups.

Within the weekly group, the people who jolted most often were the ones with the poorest sleep quality, the strongest unhelpful beliefs about sleep, and the most anxiety.

Depression scores were not linked to how often the jolts came.

Together, sleep quality, sleep beliefs, anxiety, age and gender accounted for about 27% of the differences in how often people reported sleep starts. Younger people reported them more often.

Asked what made the jolts more frequent, participants pointed to stress, tension and emotional strain. Sleep loss came up less often.

“The more strongly participants held unhelpful beliefs about sleep and the more anxious they were, the more often they reported sleep starts – and in the moment itself, many described a strong pressure to finally fall asleep,” Grünberger said.

“Our data cannot show what causes what, but this pattern resembles what we know from insomnia.”

The pressure to sleep showed up in the numbers. Among the weekly group, 83.3% said the thought “I finally have to sleep!” ran through their heads around the jolt, and 76% said they had tried to force themselves back to sleep.

Just over half of those with weekly jolts said the episodes made it harder to fall asleep. Among those who reported a delay, it averaged about 43 minutes. About 41% said the jolts made no difference.

The authors read the pattern against a well-known idea in insomnia research: the harder a person monitors and strains for sleep, the more alert they become.

In that view, the jolt and the worry about the jolt can keep each other going.

To calm the jolts, participants most often tried steering their thoughts elsewhere at bedtime, relaxation exercises, exercise, and cutting noise and light in the bedroom. They rated those as only modestly helpful.

There is no standard questionnaire for sleep starts, so the team wrote its own items from the clinical literature.

The questions have not been tested against any validated measure, and the weekly cutoff that defined the groups was chosen after the data were in.

The survey also could not separate sleep starts from look-alike experiences, such as the loud-noise phenomenon called exploding head syndrome or vivid images as sleep begins.

People answered from memory, and no one’s sleep was recorded in a lab.

“Because there is no established questionnaire for sleep starts, we developed our own items based on the clinical literature,” Grünberger said.

“This allowed us to capture a broad range of experiences – but it also means that our findings now need to be confirmed with validated instruments and objective sleep recordings.”

The next step, Schabus said, is to test whether treatments that lower arousal and sleep worry, the kind used for insomnia, also ease distressing sleep starts. No one has run that test yet.

Until someone does, the survey offers a description of the jolt and the people it troubles, and an untested idea about why.

The full study was published in the journal PLOS Mental Health.

A factory worker experimented with a pressurized air system while on the job, and it resulted in a fatal injury.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The patient: A 35-year-old man in the Czech Republic

The symptoms: The man was injured while working in a factory. His co-workers learned he'd been hurt after he crawled from the ground floor to the first floor and shouted for help. He had severe abdominal pain and rectal bleeding, and he said he had been injured while conducting "a silly experiment" involving a pressurized air system. However, he did not describe exactly what had happened.

"He repeatedly stressed that the incident was his own fault," doctors later wrote in a report of his case.

What happened next: The man was flown by helicopter to a nearby hospital, but during the flight, he became unresponsive and showed signs of hemorrhagic shock — a type of shock caused by significant blood loss over a short period. Shock, broadly, is when organs and body tissues don't receive enough oxygen due to decreased blood flow; if untreated, it can lead to organ failure and death.

Medical attendants in the helicopter worked to revive the man, but he died before he could be admitted to the hospital. Because the fatal injury occurred at the man's workplace, the police ordered a medicolegal autopsy, which both identifies the cause of death and collects details for law enforcement agencies, as part of an inquest procedure.

The autopsy: The coroner examined the body and noted that the soft tissues of the man's face were swollen and abnormally distended from retained air. The man's anus and genital areas were similarly distended and densely coated with dried blood, with radial tears in the skin surrounding the anus.

Next, the coroner conducted an internal examination. The man's brain was swollen, and he had air bubbles in his brain and chest cavity. Blood had collected around his diaphragm (the large muscle that helps inflate and deflate the lungs). It had also accumulated in the wall between the heart chambers on the left side, in tubes leading to his lungs, and in the membranes covering his lungs and heart. Reservoirs of blood also pooled in the man's abdominal cavity, in the tube leading to his right kidney, and in his digestive organs.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

The man's heart was "shrunken and empty," according to the report.

The autopsy also revealed foreign objects stuck between loops of the man's small intestine. These included three pieces of a black rubber pipe stopper and scraps of a plastic bag. His rectum — the final straight portion of the large intestine — had detached violently from his anus. It was surrounded by blood and marked with a laceration that was nearly circular, indicating that an "explosive rectal injury" had triggered hemorrhagic shock and caused the man's death, the coroner concluded.

Further investigation: Additional evidence from the factory and rubber fragments in the man's small intestine provided the police with further insight into his injuries; additional clues came from his internet search history, including photos of himself that he'd submitted to an amateur sex website.

The police concluded that the man had been performing autoerotic anal stimulation while at work, using a rubber inflatable pipe stopper measuring 2 to 3 inches (50 to 70 millimeters) in diameter, and an air gun, a handheld device for directing powerful jets of compressed air.

They suggested that the man likely attached the expandable pipe stopper to the muzzle of the air gun, which was in turn connected to the factory's air distribution system by a long, high-pressure hose. He then covered the pipe stopper with a plastic bag, inserted it into his rectal cavity, and pressed the air gun's trigger, causing "an unexpected abrupt inflation and explosive bursting of the pipe stopper within his rectum," the doctors wrote in the case report.

What makes the case unique: This case is the first recorded example of a person dying from a "rectal explosion during self-gratification," the doctors wrote. Piecing together the circumstances leading up to the man's injury was important for the hospital's doctors and law enforcement to understand how the fatality likely occurred, the authors said.

When performed responsibly and consensually, rectal insertion of foreign bodies typically does not cause significant injury, the authors added. However, "the introduction of some objects into the rectum might have unpredictable and even fatal effects."

#6489. Fatal cases of Ebola often share a striking pattern

Ebola may trap immune messages inside infected cells, keeping the body's defenses active longer and potentially worsening illness.

A deadly virus such as Ebola might be expected to kill by shutting down the body’s defenses.

Ebola virus does make proteins that block a key signal the body uses to fight infection. The pattern in patients, however, is the opposite.

People who die from Ebola often show the highest activity in the genes that fight viruses.

Scientists have struggled to explain this for years.

A new study points to the tiny droplets of protein and RNA that Ebola virus builds inside infected cells. These droplets are known as viral condensates, and the cell’s own immune messages become trapped inside them.

Once trapped, the messages are not broken down when they should be.

The defense therefore remains switched on. That prolonged response may be part of what makes patients so ill.

The findings come during a major outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo.

As of November 17, the CDC reported 11,613 confirmed cases and 5,678 confirmed deaths in the Democratic Republic of the Congo.

The outbreak involves Bundibugyo virus, a close relative of the virus studied here.

Two of them make proteins called NP and VP35. Both attach to viral RNA and to each other, gathering into droplets that have no outer membrane.

During an infection they can take up between one-fifth and one-third of a cell.

Jingru Fang led the work in the Saphire Lab at the La Jolla Institute for Immunology. Fang now works at Princeton University’s Omenn-Darling Bioengineering Institute.

“When birds land in a new place, they make nests where they can raise their babies,” said Fang.

“You can imagine viral condensates as nests for a virus.”

To study the droplets, NP and VP35 were introduced into human kidney cells. The actual virus was left out, and the droplets still formed.

The messenger RNA in those cells was then stained. Messenger RNA carries the instructions a cell uses to make a protein.

Messenger RNA was more concentrated inside the droplets than in the surrounding cell fluid.

In human cells, the buildup came to roughly 40%. Kidney cells from Egyptian fruit bats showed an even greater buildup.

When NP was changed so that it could no longer attach to single-stranded RNA, that buildup fell by about half.

A similar change to VP35 had little effect in human cells. NP appears to play the bigger role in collecting RNA.

That figure covers every message at once, and says nothing about which ones are collected.

The team therefore used a method capable of reading thousands of RNA types at once, across 136 genes linked to Ebola infection and the immune response.

About 90,000 cells were examined, with droplets found in roughly 30% of them. Of the 66 genes measured reliably, all but two were more concentrated inside.

The amount of RNA made little difference. Rare messages collected inside while far more common ones stayed out, indicating that something other than abundance determined where they ended up.

Shape proved to be the better explanation.

RNA is not always a straight strand. Parts of it join together wherever the letters match, folding the molecule into loops and stems.

Messages with fewer folds in their protein-making sections entered more readily.

To test this, the genetic instructions in some messages were rewritten. The new versions made the same protein but folded differently, and those with fewer folds entered more readily.

Ten viruses that carry negative-strand RNA were also examined, including Ebola, measles, rabies and Marburg. In all of them the protein-making regions had fewer folds than the human messages left outside.

The most striking finding concerned interferon. Type I interferon, released when a cell detects a virus, switches on hundreds of defense genes in nearby cells.

After the cells were treated with interferon, the droplets started collecting different messages.

Messages from more than 20 defense genes appeared in droplets.

The rule governing entry also changed. The protein-making section was no longer the best indicator.

Instead the tail of each message mattered more, the stretch that follows the instructions for making a protein.

Immune defense messages often have long, tightly folded tails.

The more folded the tail, the more of that message was found inside. Interferon also increases proteins that attach to RNA, and some of these may help pull immune messages into the droplets.

People who die from Ebola often show stronger activity in their defense genes than those who survive. Even people who recover can show signs of inflammation-related gene activity years later.

Erica Ollmann Saphire, who led the study with Fang, is the president and chief executive of the La Jolla Institute for Immunology.

“These are strong immune responses, but they’re not working well,” said Ollmann Saphire.

Cells normally break down messenger RNA once it has served its purpose. Enzymes such as XRN1 help carry out that cleanup.

Staining showed less XRN1 inside the droplets than in the surrounding cell fluid.

This raised a further question: whether messages trapped inside survive longer because the enzymes cannot reach them.

Messages held in the droplets broke down more slowly than the same messages in cells carrying a modified NP that could not bind RNA. Messages that stayed outside broke down at similar rates in both groups.

“The antiviral response is like a weapon, and cells use degradation as a way to deactivate that weapon,” Fang explained.

Protein production also changed. A protein the cell requires in order to start building other proteins was largely missing from the droplets.

Without interferon, more messenger RNA collected inside but less protein came out of it.

With interferon, both rose: one defense message increased more than sixfold, and levels of two defense proteins rose alongside it.

A final experiment used a weakened Ebola virus, one lacking a gene needed for replication.

A defense message called IFIT3 was found inside the droplets of those infected cells as well.

Bats can carry filoviruses without getting sick. These viruses belong to the same family as Ebola.

Bat genes cannot be read with tools designed for human RNA. Computer models were therefore used to predict how 45 of the collected messages would fold, in bats, ferrets and macaques.

Ferrets and macaques can become seriously ill from Ebola, which makes them useful comparisons.

Within the defense genes, the bat versions had tails that were less tightly folded than the human ones. Ferret and macaque tails were much more like those in humans.

Genes outside the defense group showed no meaningful difference between species.

Fever often comes with an interferon response, so the predictions were repeated at 102 degrees Fahrenheit (39 degrees Celsius).

Messages carrying bat tails then behaved as the folding had predicted. The least folded bat tail kept its message out of the droplets better than the matching human tail.

Bat immune messages may therefore be less likely to become trapped. If they remain outside, cells can break them down at the usual time.

Most experiments used kidney cells grown in a laboratory. The process was not tested in human patients or living animals, and for much of the work NP and VP35 stood in for the complete virus.

The cells were measured at just one point, 24 hours after the proteins were introduced, across 136 genes out of roughly 20,000.

The human kidney cells responded poorly to interferon. Higher concentrations were therefore used for longer periods than other tissues might need.

The RNA folding patterns were computer predictions. They cannot fully show how every RNA molecule behaves inside a living cell.

The bat comparison included only one species. It was chosen partly because scientists have not yet identified Ebola virus’s natural host.

“We don’t know whether this difference can explain everything, but it gives researchers a place to start looking and confirm what we’ve found in additional human or animal samples,” Fang added.

Breaking the droplets apart may be worth pursuing as a treatment, the authors wrote. It could slow the virus and prevent immune messages from remaining active too long.

The principal challenge is achieving that inside living cells without destroying the cells.

The full study was published in the journal Cell.

#6488. Even slightly warmer summers are linked to a higher death risk for people with heart disease

A UK study links extreme heat and repeated heatwaves to higher death risks among people with heart disease.

An average summer temperature of about 62°F (16.5°C) sounds mild. But even slightly warmer summers were linked to a higher risk of death among people with cardiovascular disease.

In a large UK study, researchers found that for every 1.8°F (1°C) increase in average summer temperature, patients had a 15% higher risk of dying from any cause.

The risk was also higher among patients who experienced more heat waves. The odds of death rose on the hottest days and after sharp jumps in temperature from one day to the next.

Taken together, the findings indicate that heat may influence survival across entire seasons in heart patients. An influence during brief hot spells is suggested as well.

The research was conducted by Ka Yan Lai of the University of Hong Kong alongside colleagues there. Further collaborators were based at the University of Oxford.

Using health records, the investigators followed nearly 64,000 UK patients for periods of up to 16 years.

Lai said the health effects of extreme heat have “rarely been studied among people with pre-existing conditions.”

All of the patients had been enrolled in UK Biobank, a long-running British health project. Half a million volunteers aged between 37 and 73 were recruited to it from 2006 to 2010.

From this pool, 63,860 volunteers were selected by the team for analysis.

All received their first hospital diagnosis of cardiovascular disease between 2006 and 2022.

Cardiovascular disease, or CVD, includes conditions that affect the heart and blood vessels.

Four of those disorders were examined on their own as well. Atrial fibrillation, an irregular heartbeat, was the first of them.

The second was ischemic heart disease, in which narrowed arteries can’t deliver enough blood to the heart. Heart failure and stroke made up the remaining two.

At diagnosis, the patients had reached an average age of about 69 years. Deaths from any cause had been recorded for 12,237 of them by the end of 2022.

That figure corresponds to roughly one patient in five.

Temperature data were taken from the daily records kept by the Met Office. Those records are mapped onto squares measuring about 0.6 miles (1 kilometer) across.

For every summer, defined as June through August, each home address was matched to its square.

Considerable variation in average summer temperature was evident across that map. The coldest squares averaged about 43°F (6.1°C), whereas the warmest reached about 66°F (18.7°C).

The central result relates to the average summer temperature at each patient’s place of residence. A 15% higher risk of death was associated with every additional 1.8°F (1°C).

Several other influences had been accounted for before that estimate was produced. Among them were age, sex, smoking, alcohol use, diabetes and neighborhood deprivation.

For patients with ischemic heart disease, each added degree Celsius corresponded to a 19% higher risk. A smaller increase of 10% was found among those with atrial fibrillation.

The results for heart failure and stroke were less certain. In both groups, the link with average summer temperature was too weak to exclude chance.

Adults aged 65 and older in New England had been examined in an earlier US study.

A 1% increase in deaths was reported there for each 1.8°F (1°C) rise in long-term average summer temperature. Older adults in general were covered by that work, not only people with heart disease.

Heat waves were also counted by the researchers. A heat wave was defined as two or more consecutive days hotter than 90% of local summer days.

Exposure to four or more heat waves a year was experienced by some patients. Their risk of death exceeded by 24% that of patients exposed to two or fewer.

Among patients with atrial fibrillation, the corresponding increase in risk was 29%. It stood at 28% among those with heart failure.

A second analysis was restricted to patients whose deaths occurred during a summer.

For each such patient, temperatures on the day of death and the five preceding days were examined. These were then compared with other days in the same month that fell on the same weekday.

Because every patient served as their own comparison, fixed traits can’t account for the results. Sex and schooling are examples of such traits.

On the hottest 1% of summer days, the odds of death among the patients as a group were 70% higher. The reference point was the temperature at which deaths were lowest.

Temperature changes from one day to the next were measured as well. The largest one-day rises were taken to be those in the top 1% of such changes.

After rises of that size, the odds of death were roughly double those seen when temperature held constant.

Roughly threefold odds were found in patients with ischemic heart disease or heart failure.

Considerable uncertainty surrounds the estimates for sharp rises. In heart failure, the plausible range extended from 36% higher odds to more than seven times as high.

No clear link with deaths was detected for sudden drops in temperature.

Events inside the patients’ bodies were not measured at any point in the study. A plausible explanation was instead drawn by the authors from earlier research on extreme heat.

In hot weather, warm blood is pumped toward the skin so that heat can be shed by the body. As much as 5 gallons (20 liters) of blood may be pumped by the heart each minute.

Sweating can meanwhile strip water and salt from the body. Blood that holds less water becomes thicker, and thicker blood may clot more readily.

In a person with heart disease, the extra pumping may require more oxygen than the heart can obtain.

Among patients lacking a college or university degree, warmer summers were tied more strongly to death. A weaker link was seen in patients who held such a degree.

A similar contrast emerged between neighborhoods with moderate green space and the greenest neighborhoods, where the link was weaker.

Among heart failure patients, the link was stronger in the most deprived neighborhoods.

Several possible reasons were put forward by the authors. Deprived neighborhoods tend to be overcrowded and to suffer more air pollution and traffic noise, they wrote.

Physically demanding work in extreme weather is also more common among people with less money.

Green spaces, meanwhile, have been shown in earlier studies to cool their surroundings.

According to Lai, protection will have to be delivered at several levels at once. City planning was named as one of those levels.

Cooling strategies form another, as do personal decisions about where to live. Lai said such protection is needed most by the most vulnerable groups.

Extreme heat is projected to grow more frequent and more intense as populations age. That observation came from study co-author Chinmoy Sarkar of the University of Hong Kong.

Together, he said, those trends will make protecting frail people with chronic diseases a top public health priority.

A link between heat and death can be demonstrated by a study of this kind. Proof that heat caused the deaths lies beyond its reach.

Because temperatures were assigned by home address, the patients’ actual whereabouts each day remain unrecorded. Nor was any information available on air-conditioning use or on changes in medication.

Smoking and drinking habits were recorded only once, when volunteers joined UK Biobank.

Those habits may well have changed afterward. Since cases were identified through hospital admissions, milder disease that never led to admission was missed.

UK Biobank volunteers may also differ from the wider population. About 96% of the patients in this study were white. The authors wrote that the volunteers may not represent everyone in the UK with cardiovascular disease.

None of the patients was given a cooler home or a greener street during the study. How many deaths such changes might prevent therefore can’t be read from the records.

Air-conditioning use could be accounted for in future research, as could travel to places with different temperatures.

The full study was published in the journal PLOS Climate.

#6487. We know how to stop computer worms. But what if AI helps them persist?

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

AI worms could spread like octopuses or slime molds, exploiting smart devices

Common forms of cyberattack include viruses and worms. Researchers recently added new styles of attack to the twisted menagerie: worms that act more like octopuses or slime molds.

VICTOR HABBICK VISIONS/SCIENCE PHOTO LIBRARY/Getty Images

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

AI is already powering new, more adaptable forms of cyberattack, but hackers typically wield the technology from afar. What if they set the AI models themselves loose to self-replicate and spread in a malicious manner?

Recent experiments have demonstrated two different ways this could happen. Two independent teams showed how a cyberattacker could turn an AI model into a “worm,” a type of malware that, unlike a computer virus, spreads on its own. And AI unlocked a new worm power: adapting attacks to different devices.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

The results hint at a new way AI could be used to ramp up cybersecurity threats — not just to computer systems but to smart devices such as security cameras or refrigerators. The good news is that the world still has time to build up defenses as several obstacles remain before this type of malware would work in the real world, says AI researcher Jonas Guan.

AI could indeed make a worm “much harder to stop,” he says, but “there are a lot of kinks to iron out before something like this really works at scale.”

Here is how a worm cyberattack works. A malware worm squirms through the internet, copying itself onto whatever systems it can hijack. Hackers can then mine hijacked systems directly for their data or link them together into a botnet and use its computing power, often to send spam email or overwhelm websites with traffic, knocking them offline.

Historically, computer worms have been small, simple programs preprogrammed to take advantage of specific security weaknesses. So they could only get into devices that had that weakness. When defenders patched a worm’s target, it could no longer spread. With an AI model directing its actions, however, a worm can adapt and learn on the fly, choosing its line of attack depending on the device, says Guan, of the University of Toronto.

That adaptability enables the worm to burrow into many different types of devices, both experiments showed. When hackers unleash AI from afar, they orchestrate what the model does. An AI worm that copies itself widely could hypothetically escape anyone’s control.

Still, there’s a caveat to the experiments’ results, says Michael Alexander Riegler, a cybersecurity researcher at Simula Metropolitan Center for Digital Engineering in Oslo, Norway. Both teams’ test environments made it easier for the AI worm to spread than it would be in the real world, says Riegler, who was not involved in either study.

And there’s another practical obstacle to the unleashing of AI worms. They use more computing power and take up more space than a conventional worm. The Mirai worm, which took down a slew of websites including Reddit and Spotify in 2016, was a few kilobytes in size, while the medium-sized AI models in the experiments were tens of gigabytes. That’s still way smaller than the massive, top-of-the-line models behind the “rogue AI” incidents that made headlines earlier in 2026. (And those weren’t worms, because they didn’t copy themselves and spread.)

Most devices — including typical laptop computers — don’t have enough space or the right kind of chips to run worm-capable AI models, Guan says. But new versions of devices, such as security cameras, are coming out with advanced hardware for running AI, researchers at the AI company Anthropic write. And at the same time, even smaller AI models are becoming more capable of sophisticated cyberattacks. These developments could expand the pool of devices an AI worm could exploit.

“The ingredients are converging” to make AI worms more realistic, Riegler says. How quickly they will converge is up for debate. Anthropic puts the timeline at months into the future, but both Riegler and Guan say it will probably take longer.

The Mirai worm spread itself through smart devices including home routers, security cameras and even baby monitors. It broke into these devices by trying a small set of common default usernames and passwords. “Just using this very simple technique, this Mirai botnet was able to infect hundreds of thousands of devices,” says cybersecurity expert Zane Ma of Oregon State University in Corvallis, who presented an analysis of the attack at a 2017 security symposium. High-profile downed sites such as Reddit were actually collateral damage: A small group of young hackers had created the worm to mess with gaming servers.

Rebooting an infected device cleared Mirai. Changing its default login credentials prevented reinfection through the same route. But an AI-powered worm might make cleaning up this type of cybersecurity breach much more difficult. Why? Because the AI worm acts more like an octopus, Guan says.

Guan and colleagues tested this octopus-worm in a virtual network. Anchored by several powerful computers that each had a chip called a graphics processing unit, or GPU, the faux networks also contained simulations of smart devices, including office printers and security cameras.

The octopus’s AI model head started on a single machine with a GPU. From there it sent out tentacles to take control of smaller devices. Upon encountering a new device, the head would use AI to plan how its tentacle could hack in. Often, a hack wouldn’t work, but the octopus wouldn’t give up. It would use info about how it failed to come up with a new hack to try. That ability is “a new, hypercharged way of attacking systems,” Riegler says. Whenever it found a computer with a large enough GPU, it would copy its head onto that new machine.

An attacker would probably launch an octopus-style AI worm from the cloud. Click through this slideshow to see how it might spread autonomously. First, it takes over and copies itself onto a device with the right kind of hardware (chip icon) to house an AI model (first image). From there, it sends out tentacles (red arrows) to hack into any connected devices, like 3-D printers and security cameras (second image). Devices that don’t have enough space for the AI model become jumping-off points for the octopus-worm to discover new places to copy itself (third image).

J. Hirshfeld; adapted from J. Guan et al/arXiv.org, 2026

J. Hirshfeld; adapted from J. Guan et al/arXiv.org, 2026

J. Hirshfeld; adapted from J. Guan et al/arXiv.org, 2026

The head could also search a simulated internet for information about newly discovered vulnerabilities. (The team didn’t connect it to the real internet for obvious reasons — protection against an AI octopus invasion — and spent considerable effort making sure their creation couldn’t escape the lab, Guan says.)

The octopus-worm even came up with a way to survive a reboot, something Guan says they hadn’t asked it to do. The team posted a preprint of their findings at arXiv.org on June 2, and the paper is now going through peer review.

Meanwhile, at Anthropic, researchers showed another way an AI worm might work by building on Guan and his colleagues’ research. If an octopus-worm wasn’t weird enough, Anthropic dubbed its creation a “digital slime mold”, a name that captures the model’s slow, oozing behavior. Anthropic declined to comment for this story, but Guan says the company’s work shows that “unlike human reasoning, AI reasoning can be distributed.” That means an AI worm wouldn’t necessarily need to hijack a powerful computer to copy and run itself — it could spread its “thinking” out among smaller devices.

And that’s exactly what the slime mold version of an AI worm does. It breaks itself up and runs pieces of the model on multiple smaller devices. In their report posted online October 12, the Anthropic researchers used 15 Android smart TVs that they had networked together.

Anthropic’s chopped-up model processes data thousands of times more slowly than what’s possible with GPUs similar to the ones Guan and colleagues relied on. That’s because the model’s data has to travel over internet connections that could take it all around the world during processing, rather than remaining in one place, within chips optimized for AI processing. That pace was too slow to demonstrate an ability to spread like a computer worm, Guan notes. So the Anthropic team ran a separate experiment with an AI worm running on GPUs that showed it could spread and adapt its attacks to different kinds of devices.

Whether AI worms are coming in months or whether we have longer to prepare, defenders should get ready now, Guan says. And AI worms do have weaknesses.

For one thing, the large size of an AI worm could be its downfall. Even if smaller AI models become more capable, these are still big programs that guzzle computing power. You might not notice if your fridge or microwave suddenly started sending lots of traffic onto the network, but your internet service provider would. They’d realize “there’s something weird going on on these devices,” Ma says. From there, they could quarantine affected devices, disconnecting them from the internet to prevent further spread.

Ma also points out that most smart devices in a person’s home aren’t directly connected to the public internet. Most home networks use a router as a central hub, and that provides a layer of protection against a worm attack.

Strong passwords, regular updates and other normal security measures would also protect against the attacks demonstrated in both experiments, Riegler says.

Guan and some colleagues are now testing specific defenses to stop AI worms, including devising an AI-driven defender. Trying to anticipate emerging threats and protect systems ahead of time is “what I’m passionate about,” Guan says. “We are working on the problem day and night.”

#6486. Ice baths after exercise: What happens when you make them a habit?

Ice baths may ease soreness after a hard workout, but regular cold plunges after lifting may limit gains in muscle size and strength.

An ice bath after a hard workout may ease muscle soreness. But taking one after every lifting session may make it harder to build muscle and strength over time.

A major review led by Edith Cowan University (ECU) found it can blunt long-term strength and muscle gains.

Researchers analyzed 15 published systematic reviews and meta-analyses. Together they covered 161 studies and more than 3,200 participants.

The takeaway is simple. Athletes, coaches, and fitness fans should be strategic, not habitual, with ice baths.

“Cold-water immersion is not a one-size-fits-all recovery tool,” said lead author Erfan Berjisian, a PhD student at ECU.

“Its benefits depend heavily on the athlete’s goals, the type of exercise completed, and when the next performance session is scheduled.”

The review found ice baths are particularly good at reducing muscle soreness. They also lower markers of muscle damage and they help athletes feel recovered faster.

Muscle soreness dropped consistently for up to four days after exercise. Markers of muscle damage were lower between 24 and 72 hours after an ice bath.

The review also noted a boost in heart rate variability right after exercise. That’s a sign the body is starting to recover.

For athletes who need to compete again soon, the benefits depend on what they’ll be doing and how much time they have to recover.

“Cold-water immersion appears especially useful when recovery time is limited, such as during tournaments, congested competition schedules or repeated high-intensity training sessions,” Berjisian said.

Researchers found endurance performance improved within the first hour after an ice bath. Power and jump performance often improved 24 to 72 hours later.

However, explosive performance actually dropped in the hours right after an ice bath.

That likely happens due to the temporary cooling effect on muscles.

“If athletes need to perform high-speed or explosive movements soon after cooling, cold-water immersion may be counterproductive unless sufficient re-warming occurs,” said co-author Kristina Kendall from ECU.

Perhaps the most significant finding was about repeated use.

Athletes who constantly used cold-water immersion after resistance training saw smaller improvements in strength, muscle size, and power.

The evidence suggests chronic use may blunt some of the body’s normal muscle-building responses to training.

The review also found a detail worth noting. The effect on strength may depend on the protocol.

Immersing just the exercised limb was linked to reduced gains. Whole-body immersion showed no clear detrimental effect.

For endurance athletes, it  was a different story. The review found no evidence that regular cold-water immersion harmed aerobic fitness or endurance adaptations.

The results suggest that cold-water immersion at 50–59°F (10–15°C) for 10–15 minutes generally helped with post-workout recovery.

Colder water, at 41–50°F (5–10°C) for the same duration, may help restore jumping performance and lower markers of muscle damage.

Both intermittent and continuous protocols worked, with no clear winner between them.

The authors also assessed the quality of that evidence. They rated it low to very low.

Most of the samples were male, which limits how well the findings apply to women.

The authors also flagged some overlap between the reviews, especially the ones on strength and muscle growth. Those conclusions rest on a fairly concentrated group of trials.

The review calls for more work on women and on different training types. It also wants research that tracks athletes over longer periods.

Ice baths may ease soreness when athletes have limited time to recover, and their effects on performance vary with the activity and the timing.

But the science says athletes should stop treating them as a cure-all.

They should be more cautious when the goal is building strength and muscle mass.

When races or matches are only a day or two apart, an ice bath may ease soreness before the next event. That can matter during a tournament, when athletes have little time to recover between rounds.

If your goal is to build muscle or get stronger, consider saving the cold plunge for competition days.

Making it a routine after lifting may limit the gains you’re training for.

The study is published in the journal Sports Medicine – Open.

A 2,000-year-old tomb was discovered in an elite burial ground of the Xiongnu, some of whom were the ancestors of the Huns.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Archaeologists have unearthed a massive 2,000-year-old tomb of an elite nomad from the Xiongnu Empire in Central Asia. The nine-level tomb contained more than 400 grave goods and is the largest Xiongnu tomb ever found in Mongolia.

Archaeologists identified the enormous tomb full of riches during a four-year excavation at the site of Duurlig Nars in northern Mongolia, according to a translated statement from the National Museum of Korea, whose researchers have been excavating the site in cooperation with the Institute of Archaeology of the Mongolian Academy of Sciences and the National Museum of Mongolia.

Duurlig Nars is the largest noble burial complex of the Xiongnu Empire, with nearly 300 ancient burial mounds called kurgans. The Xiongnu, also known as the Hunnu, were a collection of nomadic tribes who coalesced into a mobile empire on the Mongolian steppe in 209 B.C. The Xiongnu were connected to a broad trading network that stretched from the Roman Empire in the West to China and the Korean Peninsula in the East.

When the Xiongnu Empire fractured in the late first century B.C., one band moved west, picking up new tribes and eventually becoming the horde known as the Huns. Both the Xiongnu and the Huns were well known for their fighting and horseback riding skills.

The newly announced tomb is roughly square, with a long passageway extending from it, according to the statement. Including the passageway, the tomb is about 240 feet (73 meters) long, roughly the size of the Great Sphinx of Giza. Archaeologists discovered nine concentric layers of stone, each smaller than the last, going down around 48 feet (14.5 m) deep, making the tomb a kind of inverted pyramid.

Jade "bi" discs unearthed on the floor of the coffin.

A glass cup with a handle, possibly made in the Roman Empire.

Archaeologists unearthed a wooden carriage from one of the tomb layers.

In the tomb's central chamber, archaeologists found a wooden burial chamber with a coffin. The burial chamber is smaller than other elite Xiongnu burials, according to the statement, which may suggest that the society was changing and Xiongnu power was declining when the tomb was created in the late first to second century A.D.

Artifacts found in the tomb show the extent of the Xiongnu's connections across Eurasia 2,000 years ago, according to the statement. Among the grave goods recovered from the tomb were silver-and-quartz accessories crafted to decorate horses, as well as a wheel from a lacquered horse-drawn carriage, suggesting the tomb's occupant was a person of high social status.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

Additionally, archaeologists found evidence of connections with the Han dynasty, which arose around 200 B.C. and was the second imperial dynasty of ancient China. On the bottom of the wooden coffin, archaeologists recovered 15 flat, overlapping pieces of jade.

Han dynasty burials of important people often included at least one "bi," the term for a jade disk. But unlike the typically circular "bi," the jade pieces in the Xiongnu tomb are irregular and have elaborate designs engraved on them, according to the statement. This may suggest that the Xiongnu adopted a Han burial practice but put their own spin on it.

Archaeologists also found a broken cup in the tomb. The transparent glass cup with a handle may have been manufactured in the Roman Empire, the archaeologists believe. Additional tests will be carried out to try to determine where the glass cup was made.

So far, archaeologists are unsure who was buried in the tomb. But they plan to use DNA analysis techniques on the teeth and hair they recovered from the coffin to figure out the person's chromosomal sex and whether the individual was related to other people interred in the Duurlig Nars burial complex. According to the statement, future analyses of this important tomb will help archaeologists paint a more detailed picture of ancient Xiongnu society two millennia ago.

Kristina Killgrove is a staff writer at Live Science with a focus on archaeology and paleoanthropology news. Her articles have also appeared in venues such as Forbes, Smithsonian, and Mental Floss. Kristina holds a Ph.D. in biological anthropology and an M.A. in classical archaeology from the University of North Carolina, as well as a B.A. in Latin from the University of Virginia, and she was formerly a university professor and researcher. She has received awards from the Society for American Archaeology and the American Anthropological Association for her science writing.

#6482. Male bumblebees usually leave the nest, so what happens when they stay?

Lab experiments found that male bumblebees use their body heat to warm developing young, a task usually associated with queens and workers.

In a bumblebee nest, nearly all of the work has long been credited to the females.

The queen founds the colony and her daughters raise the young. Males are expected to leave soon after reaching adulthood, mate and then die.

A new study of lab-reared common eastern bumblebees has now found males helping with the young. The developing brood was warmed by the males with their own body heat.

Queens housed with males laid eggs sooner. After 28 days, nests with five males contained about 49 eggs, larvae and pupae on average, compared with 33 in nests with a queen alone.

The experiments were run by Meghan Moore and Hollis Woodard at the University of California, Riverside. Both are entomologists. Their nests were not natural ones.

Queens were housed with as many as five males and no workers, a mix rarely seen in the wild.

The project began with photos taken for a different experiment. Moore had pointed a thermal camera at the nests. Bright white patches of heat showed up on the males.

Bumblebees raise their eggs, larvae and pupae together in a single clump. Biologists call these young the brood. A queen keeps the brood warm much as a hen warms her eggs.

She straddles the clump and presses her abdomen against it. The heat is produced by muscles in her thorax, the middle part of her body.

This posture was first described in 1972 for another bumblebee species.

On each of 12 days, every nest was photographed four times within one hour. In total, 2,304 usable thermal images were collected.

The images were labeled so that scorers could not tell which kind of nest each one showed.

Males in the queen’s posture turned out to be hot. Their thoraxes averaged 94.6°F (34.8°C). Males standing on the brood without that posture averaged about 88°F (31°C).

Queens in the same posture averaged about 99°F (37.2°C). The males were not simply resting on a warm spot. Heat was being made in their bodies the way a queen makes it, only less of it.

Heat generated in the thorax is passed back to the abdomen. That rear section is the part a bee presses against the brood. Here, too, queens and males behaved differently.

In incubating queens, the abdomen was about 2.9°F (1.6°C) cooler than the thorax. In incubating males, the abdomen was 6.7°F (3.7°C) cooler. Their gap was more than twice as wide.

A possible reason was offered by the authors, who described it as speculation. Heat is known to damage sperm, including in males of another bumblebee species.

By limiting the heat that reaches his abdomen, a male may protect his sperm.

No sperm were examined in this study. For now the idea remains untested.

Moore and Woodard began the nest experiment with 75 mated queens. Each queen had been treated with carbon dioxide. This let her skip winter dormancy and begin laying eggs.

Some queens were given a nest box to themselves. Others shared a box with one, three or five young males from other colonies.

Queens living alone needed about 15 days to lay their first eggs. With one male, the wait dropped to about 11 days. It fell to about eight days with three males and about six with five.

A queen with five males therefore started laying in less than half the time of a lone queen.

Every nest was then allowed 28 days to grow, counted from its first eggs. An earlier start on egg laying could not explain a bigger nest at the end.

Fifteen queens died before the experiment was over. The brood counts come from the nests that remained.

After those 28 days, nests of lone queens held about 33 eggs, larvae and pupae on average.

Nests with five males held about 49. That is roughly 1.5 times as many. Nests with one or three males fell in between.

Only the nests with five males produced more adult workers during that time. They averaged about five workers per nest. The other groups averaged two or three.

Queens were photographed incubating about as often whether or not males were present.

The photos also showed fewer instances in which no bee was incubating the brood when males were present.

Incubation helps maintain nest temperatures, which in turn support the brood’s development. Where males were photographed incubating more often, more older brood was found at the end.

According to the authors, male incubation may directly support the growth of the brood. They also wrote that more work is needed to show cause.

Nests holding males but no workers are unusual. For that reason a smaller test was also run. Five nests containing both males and worker bees were filmed for 24 hours in darkness with infrared cameras.

Males incubated in all five nests. Two of the nests were young, with fewer than 15 bees. Two others were mature, with 50 or more.

On video, a male can be picked out by a patch of facial hair. It is sometimes described as a moustache.

Male incubation is not a new observation.

In 1985, entomologist Sydney Cameron reported that males of a different bumblebee species incubate pupae. Moore and Woodard have now added a second species.

They also measured how nests developed when males were present.

How often males do any of this in wild nests cannot yet be said. Young wild nests usually hold a queen and her workers. Males mostly appear late in the season.

The lab males were also unable to leave. Any male inclined to fly off had no way to do so. The authors wrote that this may have made the males more likely to incubate.

The bees came from commercially reared colonies, which may behave differently from wild ones. They were also given food instead of foraging for it.

Wild bumblebee nests are hard to find. As a result, data on wild colonies that produce males early are scarce.

Incubation takes a great deal of energy. What that work costs a male, in energy or in fertility, was not measured.

“What’s the trade-off? There’s no free lunch,” Woodard said.

Further studies are planned on whether caring for brood affects the males’ bodies. Future research will also need to test whether male incubation itself makes nests grow. Its importance in wild colonies is still unknown.

The full study was published in the journal Royal Society Open Science.

#6481. What makes artwork memorable? Artists put their instincts to the test

Artists found that making forgettable artwork was harder than making memorable pieces, while AI predicted viewers' memories better.

Could you make a painting that someone would look at and forget minutes later?

In an art contest, researchers gave artists a choice: Create something viewers would remember or something they would quickly forget.

In a recognition test, entries meant to be memorable were recognized more often than entries meant to be forgettable.

The memorable entries also came closer to the researchers’ target for their category.

A computer model called ResMem, trained on photographs, was better than artists and a separate group of raters at sorting the most- and least-remembered artworks.

Trent Davis and Yifei Chen carried out the study together with Wilma Bainbridge of the University of Chicago.

Bainbridge leads the Brain Bridge Lab there and is an associate professor in the Department of Psychology.

Memory was tested within minutes of the art having been seen in every part of the study.

For three months the art contest remained open to adult artists who lived in the continental United States.

Each of them was permitted to enter a single piece and had to choose a category for it. Memorable and forgettable were the two categories on offer and an artist could not enter both.

The organizers accepted only flat physical works, of which paintings, drawings, and collages are examples. Digital art and photography had been excluded under the rules that the team had drawn up.

In all, 144 submissions were received from 20 states and 86 of them met the rules. Of those 86 artworks, 62 had been entered as memorable and the other 24 as forgettable.

The first memory test was completed online by a group of 119 adults who were living in the United States. All 86 of the artworks were presented to these viewers one after another in a single long stream.

Some of the artworks were shown for a second time once at least 30 seconds had passed. The viewers had been instructed to press a key whenever they believed that an artwork had appeared before.

A score for every artwork in the contest was then worked out by the team from those key presses.

Mean scores of 0.86 and 0.79 out of 1 were obtained for memorable and forgettable entries respectively. Although modest in size, this difference was unlikely to be attributable to chance.

A high target score had been set by the team for memorable entries and a low one for forgettable entries.

It was found that the memorable entries had come closer to their target than the forgettable entries had.

The team then selected the works that had been remembered best and worst by the online viewers.

Thirty-nine of those works were shown for a month at Connect Gallery in the Hyde Park neighborhood of Chicago.

Sixty-two visitors walked through the show and were free to look at the works in whatever order they wished. They had been informed that memory was the theme of the show but not that a test would follow.

Recognition was assessed afterward in a separate room where artworks were presented to the visitors on their own phones.

A mean of 89% of the tested visitors recognized any given piece from the best-remembered group. The corresponding proportion for pieces from the least-remembered group was 70% of the visitors.

Bainbridge called the show a risky experiment for the lab. Visitors to a small exhibition about memory had been given a reason to try to remember each of the pieces.

Works from the two groups had for the most part been hung on opposite walls of the gallery.

The test was therefore repeated with 141 people at a vision science conference where paper prints were mixed together.

The works remembered best online were again recognized more often than the works that had been remembered least.

The artworks were also rated on 21 qualities by a separate group of 892 people. One of those qualities was the degree to which each artwork seemed memorable to the person rating it.

The works described as memorable by these raters were not reliably the ones remembered by online viewers. It was the goals chosen by the artists that the ratings were instead found to match.

Higher memorability ratings were given to art that people found complex, surprising, interesting, or likely to become famous.

The works that viewers tended to remember were those that raters felt able to rebuild easily in the mind. Works in which a person was shown were also remembered better whereas landscapes were remembered worse.

Works that looked digitally made were remembered better too. Every entry in the contest had nevertheless been made by hand.

“What people think is memorable is different from what actually is,” Chen said.

ResMem is a neural network, which is a kind of AI program that learns from examples. It was built in Bainbridge’s lab and was trained on nearly 70,000 photographs.

The model takes in an image and returns a score that shows how likely people are to remember it.

In an earlier study, memory for more than 4,000 paintings from the Art Institute of Chicago was predicted by ResMem.

The researchers compared three ways of predicting which artworks people would remember. They looked at the 20 most remembered and the 20 least remembered pieces.

The AI model, ResMem, correctly sorted 80% of the 40 artworks. The artists’ own choices were correct 67.5% of the time.

The separate group’s ratings correctly classified 62.5% of the artworks.

ResMem also predicted which artworks gallery visitors would remember. People’s ratings could not do this reliably.

The researchers think the AI model may perform better because it does not judge art the way people do. For example, people may assume that interesting or surprising art is easier to remember, even when that is not true.

The study did not explain why making memorable art was easier than making forgettable art.

Researchers think memorable images may share certain features that catch people’s attention. Forgettable images may not have anything in common, making them harder to create on purpose.

Artists chose whether to enter the contest and which category to compete in. Some had taught themselves to make art, while others had master’s degrees in fine arts.

Neither education nor professional experience clearly affected their success. However, the researchers had only basic information about their training.

Gallery visitors may also have been more interested in art than the people who took the online test.

The researchers want to study more highly trained artists. They also suggest tracking where people look in a gallery to better understand which artworks stay in their memory.

The full study was published in the journal Psychological Science.

#6479. Rainforest ferns from an ancient lineage have a surprisingly young family tree

An ancient lineage of rainforest ferns reveals how rising mountains and retreating wetlands may have shaped plant diversity across tropical America.

Some rainforest ferns belong to a lineage that stretches back to the age of dinosaurs. Yet roughly half its living species arose within the past six million years, as mountains rose and landscapes changed.

Researchers at the University of Turku and Aarhus University have reconstructed the history of tropical American Danaea ferns.

The findings draw on decades of work identifying ferns and establishing where they grow. That groundwork made it possible to investigate how the group spread and diversified.

“We have conducted extensive research at the University of Turku in order to understand the biodiversity of the Amazon rainforest,” said senior author Hanna Tuomisto, a professor of ecology.

“In the last 25 years, we have discovered and described 47 new Danaea species previously unknown to science, and have clarified the distribution and phylogenetic relationships of the species in the Danaea genus.”

“We have now been able to link this information to the geological and climatic history of tropical America.”

The team combined DNA evidence from 78 species with 2,289 verified records of where the ferns grow. These records helped reconstruct where ancestral ferns probably lived and the elevations they occupied.

The genetic analysis included 11 species that had not yet been formally described.

The researchers’ preferred estimate suggests that the Danaea lineage split from the lineage of its closest living relatives about 128 million years ago, during the Early Cretaceous.

The common ancestor of its surviving species lived much later, around 53 million years ago. The researchers traced that ancestor to Amazonia.

But an ancient lineage need not consist of ancient species. About half of today’s Danaea species originated during the past six million years.

This complicates a familiar explanation for tropical richness: favorable conditions allowed species to accumulate over immense stretches of time.

Persistence mattered, but the landscape also kept changing, creating opportunities for new species.

Fern diversity generally reaches its greatest heights in tropical mountain forests. Danaea follows a different pattern: Amazonia has consistently held its largest pool of species in the reconstruction.

“Mountain rainforests are home in particular to an abundance of epiphytes – plants that grow on top of other plants. Danaea ferns, on the other hand, grow on the forest floor,” said lead author Venni Keskiniva, a postdoctoral researcher at Turku.

“These research results are, in fact, similar to those obtained for trees, which are also the most species-rich in lowland rainforests.”

Where a plant lives within a forest may therefore help explain where its group becomes most diverse. Findings from one fern group cannot automatically describe them all.

The Andes still played an important role. Although Amazonia contained more species, the mountains became the leading source of dispersal to other regions.

Mountain formation affected far more than the slopes themselves. As the Andes rose, they changed rainfall patterns along with the soils developing across neighboring lowlands.

Vast wetlands once occupied much of western Amazonia. Their drainage near the end of the Miocene opened additional land for forest plants to colonize.

The resulting western Amazonian soils were generally richer in nutrients and more variable, than soils in central Amazonia.

Those differences may have encouraged plants to specialize in different environments.

The timing fits the fern history. Most new Amazonian species arising within the past six million years appeared in western Amazonia during the last three million.

New land in southern Central America also offered room for expansion. Arriving lineages frequently gave rise to additional species as the region’s landscapes developed.

The first mountain-adapted Danaea lineages appeared around 20 million years ago, following an intensification of Andean uplift. Several later spread into regions farther from the equator.

Their earlier move uphill may have helped them cope with the conditions they encountered there.

“As the plants had already adapted to the cooler climate of the mountains, it may have been easier for them to spread to areas where the temperature differences between the seasons are greater,” Keskiniva said.

Lineages that remained adapted to Amazonian lowlands tended to stay within that region.

The repeated sequence of mountain colonization followed by expansion suggests that climate tolerance influenced which routes were available.

The mountains could both separate populations and help others reach new habitats. Their role changed as the landscape rose and different fern lineages established themselves.

Assigning dates to this history was difficult. Many relevant fossils are fragmentary, and researchers disagree about where they belong in the family tree.

The team compared three dating approaches, which produced substantially different ages. It favored the reconstruction most consistent with other biological and geological evidence.

The dates remain estimates, and coinciding events do not establish a cause by themselves. Still, the findings connect the survival of ancient lineages with much younger episodes of diversification.

“The biodiversity in rainforests is the result of a long history, but its formation has also been greatly influenced by events that are relatively recent on a geological time scale,” Keskiniva concluded.

The study is published in the journal Frontiers of Biogeography.

Biologist Gonzalo Quiroga-Artigas lifts the lid on the secret life of tardigrades in stunning detail for the Nikon Small World photography awards.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

It's not often we get to peer into the tiny world of tardigrades (also known as water bears). But through his photography, biologist Gonzalo Quiroga-Artigas is unmasking the secret lives of these creatures in stunning detail.

In one photo, which won Quiroga-Artigas 12th place in Nikon's 2026 Photomicrography Competition, a tardigrade (Hypsibius exemplaris) is seen shedding its tough outer layer, known as a cuticle or an exuvium, while laying an egg in the discarded skin.

"A large part of my research involves imaging, and during the many hours I spend at the confocal microscope, I have come across some incredibly beautiful and unexpected scenes," Quiroga-Artigas, a postdoctoral researcher at the Montpellier Cell Biology Research Center in France, told Live Science in an email.

"An interesting feature of tardigrade reproduction is that some species lay their eggs inside the shed cuticle, or exuvium. The exuvium can therefore provide an additional layer of physical protection for the developing embryos."

In some species, males may place sperm inside the cuticle of a molting female before egg laying, according to National Geographic. In others, the males fertilize the eggs after they have been left inside the cuticle. And some don't even need males to reproduce at all.

"Many species reproduce through parthenogenesis," Quiroga-Artigas said, which is when an embryo develops from an unfertilized egg, also known as a virgin birth. "This means that males are not required for reproduction, and the resulting offspring are genetically very similar to their mothers," he added. The species in the photograph falls into this category.

Molting and egg laying often take place over several hours, but the shedding itself is a relatively fast process. Capturing it on camera is, therefore, no mean feat.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

"Once I had collected animals that were laying eggs, I had to fix, stain, and mount the specimens before imaging them," Quiroga-Artigas said. "I then spent a long microscopy session searching for the right specimen and the right orientation to obtain a high-quality image. Finding a specimen at exactly the right stage of molting, and in an orientation that allows the process to be clearly visualized, is largely a matter of patience and luck."

—Tardigrades survive being dried out thanks to proteins found in no other animals on Earth

—Tardigrades may hitchhike on snails ... and then suffocate in their slime

—'Sexy Mantis,' obscene orangutan and prancing sparrowhawk feature in 2026 Nikon Comedy Wildlife Awards

Photographing these animals is also challenging due to their tiny size. "Working with tardigrades in the lab requires a lot of experience with micromanipulation, as they are extremely small," Quiroga-Artigas said. "Hypsibius exemplaris, for example, is only about 250 µm [micrometers] long." That's about twice the width of a human hair.

This particular photo was taken using confocal microscopy, which uses a focused laser beam to light up one section at a time to create a detailed, high-resolution image. Quiroga-Artigas used this technique for a second tardigrade photo that was listed as an Image of Distinction in the same competition.

The second image submitted by Quiroga-Artigas to the Nikon Small World competition of a tardigrade shown from beneath.

He also received an Honorable Mention in the Nikon Small World in Motion Competition for a video of a pregnant tardigrade making contact with another tardigrade, which can then be seen pooping. However, it's not clear whether the contact between the two individuals caused this movement, Quiroga-Artigas said.

Quiroga-Artigas hopes his photography and videos give viewers an idea of just how beautiful and complex the microscopic world really is. "There are tiny animals all around us that we cannot see with the naked eye, yet they live, reproduce, grow, and undergo complex life cycles just like the animals we are more familiar with," he said.

"I will continue capturing images of tardigrades in different contexts related to my future research, without necessarily having a specific photographic goal in mind," he added. "In my experience, some of the best images I have captured were not necessarily the ones I was actively looking for."
